title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
summary: You get a list `nums` of integers and an integer `target`. The list was sorted from smallest to largest, then possibly rotated at an index you aren't told: everything from that index to the end was moved, in order, to the front. Return the index where `target` sits, or -1 if it isn't in `nums`. The search must run in O(log n) time, where n is the length of `nums`.

examples.explanation: The sorted list [2, 9, 17, 25, 30, 34, 41] was rotated to start at 30, and 9 now sits at index 4.
21 would fall between 19 and 23, but it isn't in the list.
From 1 the list is sorted up to 9, so 25 must be in the run before the break, at index 1.

constraints: The values in nums are distinct

approaches.twist: Find the sorted half around mid, and search it only if the target falls between its ends; otherwise search the other half.
Binary search for the index of the smallest value first, then run a normal binary search on the sorted piece that can hold the target.
Check every index from left to right and return the one whose value equals the target.
approaches.note: Works, but it may read every number, so it takes O(n) time. The target is O(log n).

signals.meaning: Around any mid, at least one half is still in sorted order, and a sorted half's two ends tell you right away whether the target can be inside it.
A scan is O(n). To reach log n, every check has to rule out half of what's left, rotation or not.
With no repeats, comparing a half's two ends shows whether it's sorted. With repeats, equal ends could hide where the rotation happened.

constraintReading: len(nums) is at most 5000, so the size alone would allow a scan: the O(log n) requirement is what rules out O(n). Halving 5000 numbers takes about 13 checks, and lo, mid and hi need only O(1) space. Finding the smallest value first and then searching the right piece is also O(log n): two searches instead of one.

hints.clarify: Is the list sorted? In two pieces: [30, 34, 41, 2, 9] is the sorted run 30, 34, 41 followed by the sorted run 2, 9. Pick any middle index: at least one side of it, from `lo` to mid or from mid to `hi`, has no break in it. In [30, 34, 41, 2, 9] with mid at 41, the left side 30, 34, 41 is sorted.
hints.approach: Binary search that first finds the sorted half. If `nums[mid]` is the target, you're done. Otherwise, if `nums[lo]` ≤ `nums[mid]`, the left half is sorted: the target is in it exactly when `nums[lo]` ≤ target < `nums[mid]`, so keep the left half in that case and the right half otherwise. If the left half isn't sorted, the right half is, and you test target against `nums[mid]` and `nums[hi]` the same way.
hints.whyNot: Scanning for the target is O(n). Comparing the target only with `nums[mid]`, as in a plain binary search, picks the wrong half whenever the break sits between them. Finding the rotation point with one binary search and then searching the right piece with another also works in O(log n), but it's two searches and more index math.

slots.loop: Keep going while `lo` ≤ `hi`; an empty range means the target isn't there.
slots.update: Find the sorted half: the left one if `nums[lo]` ≤ `nums[mid]`, else the right one. If the target lies between that half's ends, move inside it; otherwise move to the other half.
slots.record: Check `nums[mid]` against the target first; equal means you've found its index.
slots.return: Return mid when it matches, or -1 once the range is empty.

solution.explanation: Each step halves the range, so the loop runs about log₂ n times: O(log n) time. Only three indexes are stored: O(1) space. The break between the two runs can be on only one side of mid, so one side is always sorted, and a sorted side's two ends tell you at once whether the target can be inside it. `<=` in `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` matters when lo and mid are the same index.

events.label: check
events.say: The middle of nums[{lo}..{hi}] is nums[{mid}] = {nums[mid]}. Is it {target}?

events.label: left sorted
events.say: nums[{lo}] = {nums[lo]} ≤ nums[{mid}] = {nums[mid]}, so the left half has no break: it is sorted

events.label: right sorted
events.say: nums[{lo}] = {nums[lo]} > nums[{mid}] = {nums[mid]}, so the break is on the left: the right half is sorted

events.label: keep left
events.say: {target} lies between {nums[lo]} and {nums[mid]}, the ends of the sorted left half, so search it

events.label: keep right
events.say: {target} is outside {nums[lo]} to {nums[mid]}, the sorted left half, so it can only be on the right

events.label: keep right
events.say: {target} lies between {nums[mid]} and {nums[hi]}, the ends of the sorted right half, so search it

events.label: keep left
events.say: {target} is outside {nums[mid]} to {nums[hi]}, the sorted right half, so it can only be on the left

events.label: not found
events.say: The range is empty, so {target} isn't in nums: return -1

predict.ask: Is the left half of the range sorted?
Can the target be in the sorted left half?

related.relation: The same rotated list, but there's no target: comparing mid with the end of the range finds where the second run starts.
The same exact-match search; the rotation only changes how you decide which half to keep.
